name: Bacterial Spot
summary: A bacterial disease that makes small dark spots on tomato leaves and rough, scab-like blisters on fruit. It spreads fast in warm, wet, humid weather.
symptoms: Small dark spots on leaves, sometimes water-soaked, with yellow tissue around them.
Spots join into larger brown patches in warm, wet weather, and leaves may drop.
Small raised blisters on fruit that grow and turn rough and scab-like.
Heavy leaf loss leaves fruit open to sunscald.
causes: Bacteria of the Xanthomonas group cause the disease. They survive on crop residue and can be carried on seed and seedlings.
Splashing rain, wet handling of plants, tools and hands spread the bacteria. Warm, wet, humid weather favours it; hot, dry weather slows it.

actions.text: Remove infected plants and seedlings and destroy all infected crop residue away from the field.
Do not work among plants or handle them when the leaves are wet, so bacteria are not moved by hands and tools.
Avoid watering over the leaves. Water at the base of the plant if you can.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
Clean tools and trays used on infected plants before using them on healthy ones.

prevention: Buy clean seed and healthy seedlings from a trusted supplier.
Do not crowd plants, and mulch the soil around them.
After the season, plough or bury crop residue and remove volunteer tomato and pepper plants.
Rotate with crops that are not tomato or pepper for at least one year in fields that had the disease.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots spread quickly or you cannot tell this from other leaf spot diseases.

sources.title: Bacterial diseases of tomato - University of Maryland Extension
Bacterial speck and bacterial spot of tomatoes - Mississippi State University Extension

name: Early Blight
summary: A fungal leaf disease that shows as brown spots with ring patterns, first on the oldest leaves. It can kill leaves, damage fruit and cut yield.
symptoms: Brown dead spots on the older, lower leaves, often with a yellow halo and ring-like marks like a target.
Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wither and drop, which exposes fruit to sunscald.
Leathery spots on fruit near the stem end.
Dark stem spots on seedlings; infected seedlings may die or stay stunted.
causes: A fungus (Alternaria solani) that survives in infected plant debris in the soil and can also travel on seed.
Spores spread by wind, rain splash and overhead water. Warm, wet weather, heavy dew and plants weakened by poor fertility, drought or heavy fruit load favour it.

actions.text: Remove and destroy badly infected leaves and plant debris, and do not leave them in the field.
Scout older leaves every week, especially after rain or heavy dew, so you catch spots early.
Pull out weeds and volunteer tomato, potato, eggplant and pepper plants that can carry the fungus.
Keep plants healthy with good soil fertility and steady watering, because stressed plants get the disease more easily.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Use clean, disease-free seed and healthy seedlings.
Rotate away from tomato, potato, eggplant and pepper for at least 2 years.
Choose varieties with some resistance where your seed supplier offers them.
Plough or turn under crop debris after harvest to reduce spores near the next crop.
help: Ask your agriculture extension officer for help if leaf spotting keeps spreading despite removing infected leaves.

sources.title: Early Blight - Utah State University Extension
Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension

name: Late Blight
summary: A very fast disease of tomato and potato, caused by a water mould, that can kill whole plants within days in cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Water-soaked spots on leaves that grow quickly into large olive-green to brown patches.
White fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid or wet weather.
Brown to black spots on stems, and firm brown spots on fruit.
Plants may collapse so fast they look frost-damaged.
causes: A water mould (Phytophthora infestans), the same organism behind the Irish potato famine, causes it.
It survives on infected potato tubers, cull piles, volunteer potato and tomato plants and nightshade weeds. Wind and wind-driven rain carry the spores far.
Cool, wet and cloudy weather favours it; hot, dry weather is not suitable for it.

actions.text: Remove infected plants quickly, bag them and bury them deep or throw them away. Do not compost them.
Scout the crop often in cool, wet or foggy weather, looking at both sides of leaves and at stems.
Destroy volunteer potato plants, cull piles and nightshade-family weeds near the field.
Stake plants and keep air moving through the crop so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Spraying works best before symptoms appear.

prevention: Plant disease-free seedlings and certified seed potatoes; do not replant last year's tubers.
Choose tomato varieties with late blight resistance when available.
Avoid watering over the leaves.
Disinfect stakes and cages before reuse.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you see these spots in cool, wet weather, because the disease spreads very fast.

sources.title: Late Blight - Utah State University Extension
Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst

name: Leaf Mold
summary: A fungal disease that makes yellow patches on the upper leaf and olive-green mould underneath. It is mainly a problem in humid greenhouses and tunnels.
symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots with unclear edges on the upper leaf surface.
Olive-green mould on the underside of the leaf, under the yellow spots.
Infected leaves curl, wither and may drop; symptoms start at the bottom of the plant and move up.
Sometimes flowers die and fruit gets a dark leathery rot at the stem end.
causes: A fungus (Passalora fulva) that lives on plant debris and can come in on seed.
Spores spread by wind, water splash, tools, workers and insects.
High humidity (above about 85 percent) and long leaf wetness favour it, so it is most common in greenhouses and high tunnels.

actions.text: Remove and destroy infected plants or leaves and clear crop debris.
Lower humidity: open vents, use fans if you have them, and avoid wetting the leaves.
Stake and prune plants so air can move through them.
Clean tools and the structure well between crops.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Use clean seed from a trusted supplier.
Remove crop residue after harvest.
Choose resistant varieties when available.
Rotate crops and move tunnels from time to time so the disease does not build up.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if mould appears on many plants in your greenhouse or tunnel.

sources.title: Tomato Leaf Mold - UMass Amherst
Tomato Leaf Mold - Cornell Vegetables

name: Mosaic Virus
summary: A virus disease that mottles tomato leaves light and dark green and can distort them. There is no cure, and it spreads on hands, tools and seed, not by insects.
symptoms: Light green, yellow or white mottling on leaves, which can look like a nutrient problem.
Leaves may be curled, fan-shaped or very narrow and stringy.
Smaller plants and lower yield and fruit quality.
Some fruit show yellow rings, brown sunken spots or browning inside.
causes: Tobacco mosaic virus and tomato mosaic virus are closely related viruses with similar symptoms.
They are not spread by insects. They spread on contaminated seed, hands, clothing, pruning tools and stakes, and enter through tiny wounds.
They can last a very long time in plant debris, and hands that touched tobacco products can carry the virus.

actions.text: Remove infected plants right away and do not compost them. A virus cannot be cured once the plant is infected.
Clean tools that touched infected plants before using them on healthy plants.
Wash hands, and avoid handling plants after using tobacco products.
Do not save seed from infected plants, and use fresh pots, soil and string for each new planting.
Control weeds and keep new plantings away from infected plants.

prevention: Use certified disease-free seed.
Plant resistant varieties; check which virus is present first because some varieties resist only one.
Handle plants as little as possible, especially when pruning and staking.
Rotate crops.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer or plant clinic to confirm the virus, since other problems and herbicide damage look similar.

sources.title: Tobacco Mosaic Virus and Tomato Mosaic Virus - Utah State University Extension
Tobacco Mosaic Virus - UC IPM

name: Septoria Leaf Spot
summary: A fungal disease that causes many small round spots on lower tomato leaves, which then yellow and fall. It rarely infects fruit, but leaf loss cuts yield.
symptoms: Small round spots on the lower leaves, with a dark border and a grey-white centre.
Tiny black dots inside the spots, which are the fungus spore bodies.
Heavily infected leaves yellow, wither and drop, starting from the bottom of the plant.
Fruit are left open to sunscald after leaves fall.
causes: A fungus (Septoria lycopersici) that survives on infected tomato and related plant debris and can travel on seed.
Spores spread by rain splash, wind and people. Warm, wet weather, long leaf wetness and dense leaves that dry slowly favour it.

actions.text: Hand-pick and destroy infected lower leaves to reduce spores.
Do not work in the crop when the leaves are wet.
Water early in the day and keep water off the leaves where possible.
Stake plants and space them so air moves through the canopy.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Use disease-free seed.
Remove and destroy crop debris at season end, or plough it under.
Rotate away from tomato for about three years and control nightshade-type weeds.
Keep plants well fed so they stay healthy.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaf loss spreads up the plant.

sources.title: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Maine Cooperative Extension
Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Illinois Extension

name: Spider Mites
summary: Tiny sap-sucking mites that live under tomato leaves and cause speckling, yellowing and fine webbing. This is a pest problem, not an infection.
symptoms: Fine white to yellow speckling on leaves, later turning bronze or brown.
Tiny moving dots under the leaf; shake a leaf over white paper to see them.
Fine webbing on leaf undersides and stems when numbers are high.
Leaves yellow, dry out and drop, exposing fruit to sunscald.
causes: The two-spotted spider mite is a tiny, eight-legged mite that feeds on plant sap, mainly under leaves.
It multiplies fastest in hot, dry, dusty weather and on drought-stressed plants, and is common in tunnels and greenhouses.
High nitrogen in the leaves encourages it, and it also feeds on beans, cucumbers, peppers, eggplant and many other crops.

actions.text: Check the undersides of leaves often, especially under speckled areas, to catch mites early.
Wash mites off with a strong stream of water.
Protect natural enemies such as ladybird beetles, lacewings and predatory mites.
Check new plants before bringing them into your field or tunnel.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Keep plants healthy and avoid drought stress.
Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser.
Start checking in hot weather.
Avoid broad-spectrum sprays, which kill the natural enemies of mites.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if webbing and leaf bronzing keep spreading.

sources.title: Tomato - Spider Mites - UConn Integrated Pest Management
Tomato: Spider mites - WSU HortSense

name: Target Spot
summary: A fungal leaf disease that makes spots with ring patterns on tomato leaves, stems and fruit. It can cause heavy leaf loss in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small irregular spots with a yellow edge on the older, lower leaves.
Some spots grow and show ring patterns like a target.
Leaves yellow, collapse and die as the disease spreads to other leaves.
Long thin spots on stems, and small light brown spots with dark edges on fruit.
causes: A fungus (Corynespora cassiicola) that also infects papaya, cucumber and legumes and survives on old tomato crop remains.
Rain carried by wind spreads the spores. Warm, wet weather and overhead watering favour it.

actions.text: Remove and burn lower leaves as soon as the disease appears.
Remove some lower branches so air can move at the base of the plant.
Keep the plot free of weeds, which may host the fungus.
Avoid overhead watering.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Do not plant next to older diseased crops, and keep away from papaya if its leaves have small angular spots.
Check seedlings in the nursery and discard any with leaf spots.
Collect and burn crop residue after harvest.
Wait at least 3 years before planting tomato again on the same land.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if the spots spread across the crop in wet weather.

sources.title: Tomato target spot - Pacific Pests, Pathogens, Weeds and Pesticides

name: Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
summary: A virus spread by whiteflies that makes young tomato leaves yellow and curled and the plant stunted. Plants infected young give little or no fruit.
symptoms: Yellowing of young leaves, between the veins and at the edges.
Small crumpled leaves that curl up or down.
Stunted, bushy plants with short spaces between leaves.
Flowers drop before fruit set, so yield falls sharply.
causes: A virus (a begomovirus) carried by the adult whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), which picks it up by feeding on infected plants.
Infected plants without symptoms, such as transplants, can carry it over long distances. Other crops and weeds can also hold the virus.
Symptoms can take up to three weeks to appear after infection.

actions.text: Remove and destroy infected plants so whiteflies cannot carry the virus from them.
Hang yellow or white sticky traps in and around the field and check leaf undersides for whitefly eggs and young.
Use reflective mulch if available, because it keeps whiteflies away.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
Keep tomato away from other tomato, pepper and bean fields that may hold the virus.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties and healthy, clean seedlings.
In nurseries and greenhouses, use whitefly-proof screens.
Rotate with crops that do not host the virus.
Check that nutrient problems are not the cause: they affect the whole crop evenly, while this virus appears in patches.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer to confirm the problem, because nutrient shortages and heat can look similar.

sources.title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus - NC State Extension

name: Early Blight
summary: A fungal disease that causes brown, ring-patterned spots on potato leaves and sunken spots on tubers. Older leaves are hit first.
symptoms: Round to angular brown spots on older leaves, with dark rings like a target.
Infected leaves turn yellow, wither and drop.
Dark velvety spore growth on the spots.
Depressed, similar spots on tubers.
causes: A fungus (Alternaria solani) that survives in infected plant debris in or on the soil and on seed.
Wind and splashing rain carry the spores. Heavy dew, rain and mild temperatures favour spore production and repeat infections.
Plants stressed by poor fertility, drought or insect damage are hit harder.

actions.text: Scout older leaves for ringed spots, especially after dew or rain.
Remove and destroy badly infected plant debris away from the field.
Keep the crop well fed and watered so plants are not stressed.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Rotate crops and plough in crop remains so fewer spores are near the new crop.
Use healthy, disease-free seed tubers.
Remove volunteer potato and tomato plants.
Reduce plant stress from drought, poor fertility and insects.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spotting spreads quickly or tubers show sunken spots.

sources.title: Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension
Early Blight - Utah State University Extension

name: Late Blight
summary: A very fast disease of potato leaves, stems and tubers, caused by a water mould. It thrives in cool, wet weather and can destroy a crop quickly.
symptoms: Large olive-green to brown spots on leaves, often with fuzzy white growth underneath in humid weather.
Brown to blackish spots on stems.
Leaves dry up and plants can die; vines may rot with a bad smell.
Plants may collapse so fast they look frost-damaged.
causes: A water mould (Phytophthora infestans), the same organism behind the Irish potato famine, causes it.
It survives in infected tubers kept as seed, cull piles, volunteer potatoes and nightshade weeds. Wind and wind-driven rain carry the spores far.
Cool, wet and cloudy weather favours it; hot, dry periods do not.

actions.text: Remove infected plants, bag them and bury them deep or throw them away. Do not compost.
Destroy volunteer potato plants and do not leave cull potato piles near the field.
Scout the crop often in cool, wet weather, checking both sides of leaves and the stems.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Spraying works best before symptoms appear.
Avoid watering over the leaves.

prevention: Buy certified seed tubers and inspect them before planting; do not replant last year's tubers.
Control nightshade-family weeds near the field.
Choose resistant varieties where available.
Give plants space so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you see these spots in cool, wet weather.

sources.title: Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst
Late Blight - Utah State University Extension

name: Bacterial Spot
summary: A bacterial disease that causes dark leaf spots, early leaf drop and rough scab-like blisters on pepper fruit. It spreads fast in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Water-soaked leaf spots, often with a yellow halo, that turn dark brown and can join into blighted patches.
In dry weather, spots dry and fall out, leaving leaves tattered.
Leaves yellow and drop early, exposing fruit to sunscald.
Small raised blisters on fruit that turn brown and scab-like.
causes: Bacteria of the Xanthomonas group cause it. They live on seed, diseased seedlings, volunteer plants and crop debris.
Wind-driven rain, irrigation splash and handling wet plants spread them. Warm weather, high humidity and long leaf wetness favour it.

actions.text: Remove and destroy infected seedlings and plants.
Do not spray, tie, harvest or handle plants while they are wet.
Remove nightshade-family weeds and volunteer plants from and near the field.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
Plough or disk crop residue soon after the last harvest to help it rot.

prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy seedlings, and reject infected ones.
Use drip watering instead of overhead watering where possible.
Choose resistant varieties suited to the strains in your area.
Rotate for at least 3 years, and do not follow pepper with tomato, eggplant or potato.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots keep spreading, since no single step controls this disease.

sources.title: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato - NC State Extension
Bacterial Leaf Spot of Pepper - West Virginia University Extension

name: Blossom End Rot
summary: A disorder, not an infection, where the bottom end of the fruit turns brown and sunken. It comes from too little calcium reaching the fruit, linked to uneven watering.
symptoms: A tan to brown spot on the blossom end of the fruit, the end opposite the stem.
The spot grows and becomes sunken and leathery.
Black or watery rot may follow when other fungi or bacteria invade the damaged spot.
Affected fruit ripen faster than healthy fruit.
causes: It is a physiological disorder: calcium does not reach the developing fruit. It does not spread from plant to plant.
Soil that is too wet or too dry, high salts, and too much nitrogen, magnesium, potassium or sodium fertiliser can block calcium uptake.
Calcium moves slowly in the plant, so even a short water shortage in warm, fast-growing weather can trigger it.

actions.text: Water regularly so the root zone is never bone dry or waterlogged.
Mulch the soil to keep moisture even and limit digging near the roots.
Pick off and discard affected fruit so the plant puts energy into healthy ones.
Do not over-fertilise; too much lush growth makes it worse.
Have the soil tested, and ask your agriculture officer how to correct soil acidity or calcium if needed.

prevention: Test the soil before planting and fix its acidity as advised.
Plant in well-drained soil.
Choose varieties more tolerant of the disorder; shorter, rounder peppers usually do better than long ones.
Avoid deep cultivation that damages roots.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer for a soil test and advice if many fruit are affected season after season.

sources.title: Blossom-End Rot - New Mexico State University
Blossom-end rot of tomatoes - Oregon State University Extension

name: Frogeye Leaf Spot
summary: A fungal leaf spot of pepper that makes round spots with a pale centre and dark ring. Heavy leaf loss lowers yield and can expose fruit to sunburn.
symptoms: Small round, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn tan to white with a darker ring.
Spot centres dry out and crack or fall out.
Long spots on stems that can girdle (ring) the stem.
Leaves yellow and drop, leaving fruit open to sunscald.
causes: A fungus (Cercospora capsici, also called Passalora capsicicola) that survives on old crop debris between seasons.
Infected seed and seedlings can carry it, and overhead watering is a risk.
It prefers hot, humid weather with warm nights.

actions.text: Inspect seedlings and discard diseased ones before planting.
Remove affected leaves early, and bury or destroy diseased plants.
Use drip watering instead of watering over the leaves.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Use disease-free seed.
Rotate away from pepper, tomato and other nightshade crops for at least two years.
Bury crop debris after harvest.
Choose resistant pepper varieties where you have had the disease before.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaf spotting and leaf drop keep increasing.

sources.title: Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frogeye Leaf Spot) on Pepper - NC State Extension
Pepper - Cercospora (Frogeye) Leaf Spot - Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook

name: Powdery Mildew
summary: A fungal disease where white powder grows under pepper leaves and yellow patches show on top. Infected leaves drop, leaving fruit open to sunburn.
symptoms: White powdery growth on the underside of leaves that turns brown with age.
Yellow or brownish patches on the upper leaf surface above it.
Leaf edges curl upward, showing the powder.
Older leaves drop, exposing fruit to sunburn.
causes: A fungus (Leveillula taurica) that grows mostly inside the leaf and makes spores on the underside. It also infects tomato, eggplant, onion, cotton and many weeds.
Wind spreads the spores and infection can repeat every 7 to 10 days. Infected seedlings may show nothing for 18 to 21 days.
It develops across a wide range of warm temperatures; humidity helps spores germinate.

actions.text: Scout the undersides of leaves regularly, especially in warm weather, because early signs are easy to miss.
Remove badly affected leaves or plants and clear weeds that can host the fungus.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Treatment works best early in the infection.
Check seedlings for symptoms before planting, since the disease can arrive on transplants.

prevention: Start with healthy seedlings from a trusted source.
Keep the field and its edges free of weeds that host the fungus.
Do not rely on field cleaning alone because the fungus has many hosts.
Keep checking the crop through the warm season.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if white powder or yellow patches appear on several plants.

sources.title: Powdery Mildew on Peppers - UC IPM
Powdery Mildew of Pepper - Cornell Vegetables
